title: War of Geniuses
reviewNotes: Six branches begin after Ra6+ at 14s, with all seven pieces reconstructed. Ba3/Rxa3/Kb2 avoids the immediate Rf6 blockade and enables the king walk. Taking Ra2 gives a bishop fork and draw; taking Rg4 reaches a drawn pawn ending. After Kh6, Kxg6/Bxf5/Kf6 instead preserves a win. Ne7 before fxg8=Q/Bxg8 produces actual Ng6 mate. Immediate capture-promotion instead draws. Every encoded step is exact-checked; Rg4 is correctly written with check.
transcript: White is only one step away from getting a new queen, and it doesn't seem like the rook can stop it. If he tries to go here, bishop to b2 is going to pin it to the king, and white would win. But, black does have a way to keep the game going, and that is to check the king. If king to b2, this prevents the bishop from going there, so the rook can go back and stop the pawn. And, if king to b1, we would lose the knight with check, and then still be forced to b2, losing like this. So, white has to get creative here, and the only way to keep the advantage going is bishop to a3, a brilliant find. Giving up the bishop seemingly for nothing, but notice something very important. Now, after king to b2, the rook cannot go back to f6, and there aren't any safe checks that can be given with the rook. Or at least, you would think so, because black has a counter brilliancy. Rook to a2 check. If the rook is taken, now bishop e6 is a fork, picking up the pawn and drawing the game. So, the rook cannot actually be taken, and white has to start walking with the king, king to c1, and the rook has to keep checking the king. The king runs, and the rook checks, and it keeps going like this, until finally we play king to g5, and shielded by the white knight, it seems like white is finally able to prepare the promotion. But, black has not run out of tricks quite yet. Rook g4. Because, of course, if the rook is taken, after this bishop check, the black king is going to stop [music] the promotion, and this is actually a drawn king and pawn endgame. So, white cannot accept the sacrifice of the rook, and instead, he should keep going up with the king. And, it seems like white is simply out of the woods. If this rook check, we can just take with the knight, and this time the rook sacrifice doesn't work. After king takes and bishop takes, we don't have to recapture the bishop, we can just play king to f6, and the king has no way to stop the pawn and the light square bishop neither. So, it seems like white is simply going to win, right? Well, not exactly. Black has one last incredible resource. The majestic rook to G8. A last Hail Mary trying to stop that pawn because of course, if we take the rook after the king takes back, we're left with knight and bishop and there is [music] no way to force a checkmate. But, black shouldn't rest easy quite yet because white has knight to E7 threatening to promote [music] with the support of the knight. So, black has to play bishop to E6 and defend that promotion square. You see white now promotes to the queen and you may think, "Pietro, you just told us that knight and bishop is going to be a draw." But, in this specific situation, the king is cornered and his own bishop betrays him as knight to G6 is a checkmate. [music]
